title: The Aeneid
author: Virgil
openingChapterLabel: Book I — Arms and the Man
openingText: I sing of arms and of the man who, forced by fate and by the unrelenting hatred of haughty Juno, was expelled and exiled from the Trojan shore. He endured long labors both by sea and land, and fought a doubtful war before he won the realm of Latium and built the destined town. He restored his banished gods to their sacred rites, and established a secure succession in his line, from which came the race of Alban fathers and the long glories of majestic Rome. O Muse, tell me the causes and the crimes! What goddess was provoked, and what kindled her hatred? For what offense did the Queen of Heaven begin to persecute so brave and just a man, entangling his anxious life in endless cares, exposing him to want, and hurrying him into wars? Can heavenly minds harbor such high resentment, or exercise their spite in human suffering?
about:
Aeneas escapes the fall of Troy with his family, his household gods, and a group of survivors. On the journey toward Italy he meets Dido, who is building Carthage. The gods demand that he continue, bringing his obligations to his people into conflict with her love and his own attachments. In the underworld, his father Anchises shows him a future reaching forward to Rome. When the Trojans arrive in Latium, their hope for a home threatens people who already live there.

Virgil wrote the twelve books of the Aeneid in Latin during the final decades of the first century BCE, under Augustus. Its voyages and battles engage closely with Homer and place the story in Rome’s mythical prehistory. Aeneas establishes the settlement and line from which Roman tradition traces its origins. The founding of Rome itself belongs to later generations.

The historical English text here is John Dryden’s 1697 translation. Each book opens with his prose summary of its events. The modern English keeps that edition’s structure and much of its rhetorical character, with specific corrections documented separately. Read for the sweep of the story and for the moments when an individual loss interrupts the advance toward the promised future.

angleCards.title: The price of destiny
angleCards.text: The gods promise a great future. Notice who pays for it and who gets to choose.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine fate, choice, and responsibility in Aeneas’s journey.

angleCards.title: Dido’s perspective
angleCards.text: Dido has already lost a home and built a new city. Her story parallels Aeneas’s and reveals what his departure means for others.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Dido’s voice and consider the space the poem gives her hopes and anger.

angleCards.title: The conversation with Homer
angleCards.text: The journeys in the first half recall the Odyssey, and the battles in the second recall the Iliad. Familiar scenes acquire new consequences.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to see how Virgil reshapes Homer’s heroes, journeys, and battles.

angleCards.title: Duty and anger
angleCards.text: Pietas encompasses obligations to gods, family, and community. Follow its encounters with grief, love, and revenge.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Aeneas’s actions with attention to both his sense of duty and his anger.

cast.name: Aeneas
cast.description: Son of Venus and Anchises, father of Ascanius, and a survivor of Troy’s fall. He bears responsibility for bringing his people to a new home. Loss and anger repeatedly test his sense of duty.

cast.name: Dido
cast.description: After her husband’s murder she fled Tyre and founded Carthage. She welcomes the Trojans. Her relationship with Aeneas becomes decisive for her life and for the mythical relationship between Carthage and Rome.

cast.name: Turnus
cast.description: A young Italian warrior and suitor of Lavinia. Amata favors their marriage, while omens point toward a foreign husband. He leads resistance to Aeneas and embodies courage, pride, and destructive anger.

cast.name: Juno
cast.description: She hates the Trojans and fears for the future of her beloved Carthage. She provokes the storm and drives the war in Italy. Her negotiation with Jupiter helps shape the people who will emerge from the conflict.

cast.name: Venus
cast.description: The goddess of love protects her son, pleads on his behalf, and persuades Vulcan to forge his weapons. Her interventions also shape other people’s lives.

cast.name: Anchises
cast.description: Aeneas carries him out of Troy. He dies on the journey but meets his son again in the underworld and shows him the future Roman generations.

whyItMatters.title: The cost of a home
whyItMatters.body: Troy’s refugees seek safety, but their arrival in Italy brings a new war. The poem connects the longing for a home with conquest and gives attention to both newcomers and those defending their land.

whyItMatters.title: The dead have names
whyItMatters.body: Amid great battles, the narrative pauses over parents, children, and lost homes. Pallas, Lausus, and Camilla each receive a distinct story. Notice how these lives change the meaning of victory.

whyItMatters.title: An ending to discuss
whyItMatters.body: The poem ends when Aeneas kills Turnus. Memory of Pallas, the desire for revenge, and the possibility of restraint meet in that moment. The ending leaves the reader to consider the relationship between the promised peace and the act that ends the war.
